questions.question: Which of the following are the main sources of biofertilisers?
questions.explanation: The main sources of biofertilisers are bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria. These organisms enrich the nutrient quality of the soil.

questions.question: Which bacteria form nodules on the roots of leguminous plants through symbiotic association?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria form nodules on the roots of leguminous plants through symbiotic association and fix atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms.

questions.question: Which of the following bacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen while free-living in the soil?
questions.explanation: Azospirillum and Azotobacter are free-living bacteria in the soil that can fix atmospheric nitrogen, thus enriching the nitrogen content of the soil.

questions.question: What is the term for the symbiotic association between fungi and plant roots?
questions.explanation: Mycorrhiza is the symbiotic association between fungi and plant roots. Many members of the genus Glomus form mycorrhiza.

questions.question: Which genus of fungi is commonly associated with mycorrhiza formation?
questions.explanation: Many members of the genus Glomus form mycorrhiza. The fungal symbiont absorbs phosphorus from soil and passes it to the plant.

questions.question: What nutrient does the fungal symbiont in mycorrhiza absorb from the soil and pass to the plant?
questions.explanation: The fungal symbiont in mycorrhiza absorbs phosphorus from soil and passes it to the plant.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit shown by plants having mycorrhizal associations?
options: Overall increase in plant growth and development
questions.explanation: Plants with mycorrhizal associations show resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, and overall increase in growth. Nitrogen fixation is not a benefit of mycorrhiza; it is associated with Rhizobium.

questions.question: Which of the following cyanobacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria can fix atmospheric nitrogen and serve as important biofertilisers in paddy fields.

questions.question: In which type of fields do cyanobacteria serve as an important biofertiliser?
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria serve as an important biofertiliser in paddy fields. They also add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility.

questions.question: What additional benefit do blue green algae provide to the soil besides acting as biofertilisers?
options: They add organic matter to the soil
questions.explanation: Blue green algae (cyanobacteria) add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility, besides acting as biofertilisers.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of using biofertilisers over chemical fertilisers?
options: They act faster than chemical fertilisers
questions.explanation: The use of chemical fertilisers contributes significantly to environmental pollution. Biofertilisers help reduce this pollution and dependence on chemicals.

questions.question: Which type of farming approach uses biofertilisers to replenish soil nutrients?
questions.explanation: Organic farming uses biofertilisers to replenish soil nutrients and reduce dependence on chemical fertilisers.

questions.question: What do Rhizobium bacteria fix from the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms, which is used by the plant as nutrient.

questions.question: What is the primary role of biofertilisers in agriculture?
options: To enrich the nutrient quality of the soil
questions.explanation: Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. They help replenish soil nutrients naturally.

questions.question: Which of the following is a free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium found in soil?
questions.explanation: Azotobacter is a free-living bacterium in the soil that can fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil's nitrogen content.

questions.question: Which antibiotic was the first to be discovered and was a chance discovery by Alexander Fleming?
questions.explanation: Penicillin was the first antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming when he observed a mould (Penicillium notatum) growing on a culture plate that inhibited the growth of Staphylococci bacteria.

questions.question: What does the term 'antibiotic' literally mean in Greek?
options: Against life (in context of disease-causing organisms)
questions.explanation: The term antibiotic comes from Greek where 'anti' means against and 'bio' means life, together meaning 'against life' in the context of disease-causing organisms.

questions.question: Who were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945 for the discovery and development of Penicillin?
questions.explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered Penicillin, but its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey. All three were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945.

questions.question: Which disease was extensively treated with Penicillin during World War II?
questions.explanation: Penicillin was extensively used to treat American soldiers wounded in World War II, saving many lives from bacterial infections.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases was NOT mentioned as being treated with antibiotics?
questions.explanation: The text mentions antibiotics have improved treatment of plague, whooping cough (kali khansi), diphtheria (gal ghotu), and leprosy (kusht rog). Diabetes is not mentioned.

questions.question: What is the full form of BOD in sewage treatment?
questions.explanation: BOD stands for Biochemical Oxygen Demand, which refers to the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all organic matter in one liter of water were oxidised by bacteria.

questions.question: What does a higher BOD value indicate about waste water?
questions.explanation: The greater the BOD of waste water, the more is its polluting potential. Higher BOD means more organic matter is present, requiring more oxygen for decomposition.

questions.question: Which sample in the BOD test exercise had the highest value of 400 mg/L?
questions.explanation: Untreated sewage water contains the highest amount of organic matter and microbes, so it would have the highest BOD value of 400 mg/L.

questions.question: What is the BOD value of secondary effluent discharged from a sewage treatment plant?
questions.explanation: After secondary treatment, most organic matter is removed by aerobic microbes, so the BOD is significantly reduced to 20 mg/L.

questions.question: Which of the following is produced by microbes during anaerobic digestion in sludge digesters?
questions.explanation: During anaerobic digestion in sludge digesters, bacteria produce a mixture of gases including methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide, collectively called biogas.

questions.question: What is the role of activated sludge in secondary treatment?
options: It is used as fertilizer directly
A small part is used as inoculum in the aeration tank
It is used for drinking water purification
questions.explanation: A small part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to serve as inoculum (starter culture), while the rest is sent to anaerobic digesters.

questions.question: Which bacteria are collectively called methanogens?
questions.explanation: Methanogens are bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce large amounts of methane along with CO2 and H2.

questions.question: Where are methanogens commonly found in cattle?
questions.explanation: Methanogens are present in the rumen (a part of stomach) of cattle, where they help break down cellulose in the food.

questions.question: What is the common name for biogas produced from cattle dung?
questions.explanation: Biogas produced from cattle dung (gobar) is commonly called gobar gas in India.

questions.question: Which Indian organizations mainly developed biogas technology?
questions.explanation: The technology of biogas production was developed in India mainly due to the efforts of Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of primary treatment in sewage treatment plants?
options: Physical removal of particles through filtration and sedimentation
questions.explanation: Primary treatment involves physical removal of particles - large and small - from sewage through filtration and sedimentation.

questions.question: What are flocs in the secondary treatment of sewage?
options: Masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures
questions.explanation: Flocs are masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments to form mesh-like structures that consume organic matter in the effluent.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of biogas?
questions.explanation: Biogas is a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide. Oxygen is not a component of biogas.

questions.question: What happens to the spent slurry from a biogas plant?
questions.explanation: The spent slurry removed from the biogas plant through an outlet may be used as fertilizer, making it a valuable by-product.

questions.question: Why can untreated sewage not be discharged directly into rivers?
options: It contains large amounts of organic matter and pathogenic microbes
questions.explanation: Untreated sewage contains large amounts of organic matter and many pathogenic microbes, which would pollute rivers and increase water-borne diseases.

questions.question: What does the term 'Biocontrol' refer to?
options: Use of chemicals to kill insects
Use of biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests
Use of weedicides to remove weeds
Use of pesticides to protect crops
questions.explanation: Biocontrol refers to the use of biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests, as opposed to chemical methods.

questions.question: Which bacteria is commonly used as a microbial biocontrol agent against butterfly caterpillars?
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is used to control butterfly caterpillars. Its dried spores are mixed with water and sprayed on plants; when eaten by larvae, a toxin is released killing them.

questions.question: How is Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) available for use as a biocontrol agent?
options: As a liquid solution ready to spray
As dried spores in sachets mixed with water
As a powder mixed directly into soil
As a gel applied to leaves
questions.explanation: Bt is available in sachets as dried spores which are mixed with water and sprayed onto vulnerable plants such as brassicas and fruit trees.

questions.question: Where does Bacillus thuringiensis toxin act in the insect body?
options: In the brain of the larvae
On the outer skin of the larvae
In the gut of the larvae
In the blood of the larvae
questions.explanation: In the gut of the larvae, the Bt toxin is released and the larvae get killed. The toxin specifically acts inside the digestive system of the larvae.

questions.question: Which insect is mentioned as useful for controlling aphids?
questions.explanation: The Ladybird beetle with red and black markings is useful to get rid of aphids. It is a natural predator that keeps aphid populations under control.

questions.question: Which insect is mentioned as useful for controlling mosquitoes?
questions.explanation: Dragonflies are mentioned as useful insects to get rid of mosquitoes through natural predation.

questions.question: Which fungus is being developed as a biological control agent against plant diseases?
questions.explanation: Trichoderma species are free-living fungi very common in root ecosystems and are effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens.

questions.question: What type of organisms are Baculoviruses known to attack?
questions.explanation: Baculoviruses are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods, making them useful for species-specific biological control.

questions.question: To which genus do most baculoviruses used as biological control agents belong?
questions.explanation: The majority of baculoviruses used as biological control agents are in the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus. They are used for narrow spectrum insecticidal applications.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of using Baculoviruses as biocontrol agents?
options: They kill all insects including beneficial ones
They have no negative impacts on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects
They are cheap and easy to synthesize chemically
They remain active in soil for decades
questions.explanation: Baculoviruses are narrow-spectrum agents shown to have no negative impacts on plants, mammals, birds, fish, or non-target insects, making them safe for ecosystems.

questions.question: What is Bt-cotton?
options: Cotton plants into which B. thuringiensis toxin genes have been introduced
Cotton plants grown near Bacillus bacteria in soil
Cotton soaked in Bt spore solution before planting
questions.explanation: Scientists introduced B. thuringiensis toxin genes into cotton plants through genetic engineering. These Bt-cotton plants are resistant to attack by insect pests.

questions.question: What does IPM stand for in the context of biocontrol?
questions.explanation: IPM stands for Integrated Pest Management, which is an overall programme where beneficial insects are conserved and biocontrol strategies are combined for effective pest control.

questions.question: According to organic farming principles, what is the role of biodiversity in pest control?
options: More biodiversity means more pest attacks
Biodiversity furthers health and makes the landscape more sustainable
Biodiversity has no connection to pest management
Biodiversity should be reduced to protect crops
questions.explanation: A key belief of the organic farmer is that biodiversity furthers health. The more variety a landscape has, the more sustainable it is, helping maintain natural checks on pests.

questions.question: Why does the organic farmer believe pests should not be completely eradicated?
options: Because without pests, beneficial predatory insects that depend on them would not survive
Because complete eradication is too expensive
questions.explanation: The organic farmer holds the view that eradication of pests is undesirable because beneficial predatory and parasitic insects depend on pests as food or hosts and would not survive without them.

questions.question: What is the main problem with using insecticides and pesticides in conventional farming?
options: They are too expensive for most farmers
They are only effective against a few pest species
They are toxic and harmful to humans, animals, and pollute the environment
They need to be reapplied every day
questions.explanation: Chemical insecticides and pesticides are toxic and extremely harmful to human beings and animals alike, and have been polluting soil, groundwater, fruits, vegetables and crop plants.

questions.question: Which type of bacteria are collectively called methanogens?
options: Aerobic bacteria that grow on cellulosic material
Anaerobic bacteria that produce large amounts of methane along with CO2 and H2
Bacteria found only in the rumen of cattle
Bacteria that require oxygen to break down cellulose
questions.explanation: Methanogens are bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce large amounts of methane along with CO2 and H2. These bacteria are commonly found in anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and in the rumen of cattle.

questions.question: What is the common name for biogas produced from cattle dung?
questions.explanation: The excreta (dung) of cattle, commonly called gobar, is rich in methanogen bacteria. Therefore, the biogas produced from cattle dung is commonly called gobar gas.

questions.question: Where are methanogens commonly found besides anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment?
questions.explanation: Methanogens are commonly found in the anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment. They are also present in the rumen (a part of stomach) of cattle, where they help in the breakdown of cellulose.

questions.question: What is the main component of biogas?
questions.explanation: Biogas is a mixture of gases containing predominantly methane. It is produced by microbial activity and can be used as fuel.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common methanogen bacterium mentioned in the text?
questions.explanation: Methanobacterium is mentioned as one common bacterium among the methanogens. Lactobacillus is a lactic acid bacterium, Saccharomyces cerevisiae is brewer's yeast, and Penicillium notatum produces penicillin.

questions.question: What happens to the floating cover in a biogas plant as gas is produced?
options: It sinks down into the slurry
questions.explanation: In a biogas plant, a floating cover is placed over the slurry, which keeps on rising as the gas is produced in the tank due to microbial activity.

questions.question: What can the spent slurry from a biogas plant be used for?
options: As a source of drinking water
questions.explanation: The spent slurry is removed through another outlet and may be used as fertiliser. This makes biogas plants environmentally friendly as they produce both fuel and organic fertiliser.

questions.question: Which Indian institutions were mainly responsible for developing biogas production technology?
questions.explanation: The technology of biogas production was developed in India mainly due to the efforts of Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).

questions.question: What is the depth of the concrete tank in a typical biogas plant?
questions.explanation: The biogas plant consists of a concrete tank that is 10-15 feet deep, in which bio-wastes are collected and a slurry of dung is fed.

questions.question: What are the main uses of biogas in rural areas?
questions.explanation: The biogas thus produced is used for cooking and lighting in rural areas. Cattle dung is available in large quantities in rural areas where cattle are used for various purposes.

questions.question: Why are biogas plants more often built in rural areas?
options: Because cattle dung is available in large quantities in rural areas
Because urban areas have better technology
Because rural areas have more electricity
questions.explanation: Biogas plants are more often built in rural areas because cattle dung is available in large quantities there, as cattle are used for a variety of purposes in rural settings.

questions.question: What role do methanogens play in the nutrition of cattle?
options: They produce vitamins for the cattle
They help in the breakdown of cellulose in the rumen
They digest proteins in the cattle's diet
They absorb water from the food
questions.explanation: In the rumen, methanogens help in the breakdown of cellulose and play an important role in the nutrition of cattle. A lot of cellulosic material is present in the food of cattle.

questions.question: Which gas is NOT mentioned as a component of biogas in the text?
questions.explanation: The text mentions that biogas contains predominantly methane, along with CO2 and H2. Oxygen is not mentioned as a component of biogas.

questions.question: What is the function of the gas-holder in a biogas plant?
options: To filter impurities from the gas
questions.explanation: The gas-holder is the part of the biogas plant that collects and stores the produced biogas (CH4 + CO2 + other gases) before it is supplied through the outlet pipe.

questions.question: What is fed into the concrete tank of a biogas plant along with bio-wastes?
questions.explanation: The biogas plant consists of a concrete tank in which bio-wastes are collected and a slurry of dung is fed. The dung provides the methanogen bacteria needed for biogas production.

questions.question: Microbes are present in which of the following extreme environments?
options: Only in mild soil and water
Deep inside geysers where temperature may reach 100C
questions.explanation: According to the chapter, microbes survive even in extreme conditions such as deep geysers (thermal vents) with temperatures as high as 100C. This demonstrates their extraordinary adaptability.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a type of microbe in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists protozoa, bacteria, fungi, microscopic plant and animal viruses, viroids, and prions as microbes. Nematodes are not microscopic microbes of this classification.

questions.question: Prions are described in the chapter as:
questions.explanation: The chapter specifically defines prions as proteinaceous infectious agents, distinguishing them from other microbes which contain nucleic acids.

questions.question: Where are microbes NOT found according to the chapter introduction?
questions.explanation: The chapter states microbes are found in soil, water, air, inside bodies, geysers, deep soil, under thick snow, and acidic environments. Outer space is not mentioned as a location.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of growing microbes on nutritive media in laboratories?
options: To form visible colonies useful for studying micro-organisms
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that bacteria and many fungi can be grown on nutritive media to form colonies visible to the naked eye, and such cultures are useful in studies on micro-organisms.

questions.question: Which kingdoms of living organisms contain micro-organisms according to the chapter's question to students?
options: Multiple kingdoms - students are asked to recall
questions.explanation: The chapter poses a reflective question asking students to recall from Class XI which kingdoms contain micro-organisms and which are exclusively microscopic, implying multiple kingdoms are involved.

questions.question: The chapter is titled 'Microbes in Human Welfare'. What does this title suggest?
options: All microbes are harmful to humans
Microbes have beneficial roles for humans despite some being pathogenic
Microbes are only found inside humans
questions.explanation: Chapter 8 focuses on beneficial roles of microbes. The introduction acknowledges that while some microbes cause diseases (Chapter 7), many are useful to humans in diverse ways.

questions.question: Viroids differ from viruses in that viroids are:
options: Listed separately from viruses in microbe classification
questions.explanation: The chapter lists viroids separately from viruses, indicating they are distinct entities. Viroids are infectious RNA particles without a protein coat, unlike typical viruses.

questions.question: What is the significance of microbes surviving under layers of snow several metres thick?
options: It demonstrates their ability to survive in extreme cold and dark environments
They produce heat energy under snow
questions.explanation: Microbes surviving under thick snow layers is cited as evidence of their extraordinary adaptability to extreme environments where no other life forms could exist.

questions.question: What are the six major topics covered in Chapter 8 according to its table of contents?
options: Genetics, Evolution, Ecology, Physiology, Taxonomy, Biochemistry
Household Products, Industrial Products, Sewage Treatment, Biogas, Biocontrol Agents, Biofertilisers
Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi, Protozoa, Algae, Prions
Food, Medicine, Water, Energy, Agriculture, Industry
questions.explanation: The chapter contents list exactly these six sections: 8.1 Household Products, 8.2 Industrial Products, 8.3 Sewage Treatment, 8.4 Biogas Production, 8.5 Biocontrol Agents, 8.6 Biofertilisers.

questions.question: Which microorganisms are commonly called Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB)?
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus and other related bacteria are collectively called Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB). They grow in milk and convert it to curd.

questions.question: What process do LAB carry out when converting milk to curd?
options: They produce CO2 which solidifies the milk
They produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins
They add vitamin C to the milk
They remove water from the milk
questions.explanation: LAB produce acids during growth that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins, thereby converting milk to curd.

questions.question: Which vitamin's level is increased in curd compared to fresh milk?
questions.explanation: The conversion of milk to curd by LAB improves its nutritional quality by increasing the level of Vitamin B12.

questions.question: What is the role of LAB in the human stomach?
options: They play a beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes
questions.explanation: In the human stomach, LAB play a very beneficial role in checking or inhibiting the growth of disease-causing microbes.

questions.question: Why does dough used for making idli and dosa have a puffed-up appearance?
options: Due to addition of baking powder
Due to production of CO2 gas by bacteria
questions.explanation: The dough for idli and dosa is fermented by bacteria, and the puffed-up appearance is due to the production of CO2 gas during fermentation.

questions.question: Which yeast is used for fermenting dough to make bread?
questions.explanation: Baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is used for fermenting the dough used to make bread.

questions.question: What is 'Toddy' and how is it made?
options: A solid food made by drying bamboo shoots
A traditional drink made by fermenting sap from palms
A cheese variety made using fungi
A bread variety made using baker's yeast
questions.explanation: Toddy is a traditional drink of some parts of southern India, made by fermenting sap collected from palms using microbes.

questions.question: What causes the large holes in Swiss cheese?
options: Production of large amounts of CO2 by Propionibacterium sharmanii
questions.explanation: The large holes in Swiss cheese are due to the production of a large amount of CO2 by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii during fermentation.

questions.question: How is Roquefort cheese given its particular flavour?
options: By ripening it with a specific fungus grown on it
By adding LAB to the milk
questions.explanation: Roquefort cheese is ripened by growing a specific fungus on it, which gives it its characteristic and particular flavour.

questions.question: What are fermentors used for in industrial production?
options: To grow microbes in very large vessels for industrial-scale production
questions.explanation: Fermentors are very large vessels used in industrial-scale production to grow microbes that synthesise valuable products like beverages and antibiotics.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a product made using microbial fermentation mentioned on this page?
questions.explanation: Butter is not mentioned as a product made by microbial fermentation on this page. Curd, cheese, toddy and bread dough are the fermented products discussed.

questions.question: What does a small amount of curd added to fresh milk as inoculum contain?
questions.explanation: A small amount of curd added to fresh milk as an inoculum or starter contains millions of LAB, which multiply at suitable temperatures to convert milk to curd.

questions.question: Which yeast is commonly used for fermenting malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol?
questions.explanation: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, also called brewer's yeast, is used to ferment malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol.

questions.question: Which alcoholic beverages are produced WITHOUT distillation?
questions.explanation: Wine and beer are produced without distillation, while whisky, brandy, and rum require distillation of the fermented broth.

questions.question: Penicillin was discovered by chance when Alexander Fleming observed a mould inhibiting which bacterium?
questions.explanation: Fleming observed a mould (Penicillium notatum) growing in an unwashed culture plate around which Staphylococci could not grow, leading to the discovery of Penicillin.

questions.question: Who established the full potential of Penicillin as an effective antibiotic after Fleming's initial discovery?
questions.explanation: Ernest Chain and Howard Florey established the full potential of Penicillin as an effective antibiotic. Fleming, Chain, and Florey jointly received the Nobel Prize in 1945.

questions.question: In which year did Fleming, Chain, and Florey receive the Nobel Prize for the discovery of Penicillin?
questions.explanation: Fleming, Chain, and Florey were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945 for the discovery and development of Penicillin as an antibiotic.

questions.question: Penicillin was named after which mould?
questions.explanation: Fleming named the antibiotic Penicillin after the mould Penicillium notatum, from which the inhibitory chemical substance was produced.

questions.question: Antibiotics are chemical substances that can kill or retard the growth of which organisms?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics are chemical substances produced by some microbes that can kill or retard the growth of other disease-causing microbes.

questions.question: Penicillin was extensively used to treat soldiers wounded in which war?
questions.explanation: Penicillin was extensively used to treat American soldiers wounded in World War II, saving countless lives.

questions.question: What type of product is Penicillin classified as?
questions.explanation: Penicillin is classified as an antibiotic - a chemical substance produced by a microbe (Penicillium notatum) that inhibits or kills disease-causing bacteria.

questions.question: The word 'anti' in antibiotic is derived from Greek and means what?
questions.explanation: The Greek word 'anti' means 'against'. Combined with 'bio' (life), antibiotic means 'against life' in the context of disease-causing organisms.

questions.question: Which fermented beverage requires distillation during its production?
questions.explanation: Whisky (along with brandy and rum) requires distillation of the fermented broth, unlike wine and beer which are produced without distillation.

questions.question: What is the common name for Saccharomyces cerevisiae used in beverage production?
questions.explanation: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is commonly called brewer's yeast when used for fermenting malted cereals and fruit juices for alcoholic beverage production.

questions.question: Antibiotics have helped treat which of the following deadly diseases?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics greatly improved the capacity to treat deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria, and leprosy which used to kill millions globally.

questions.question: Large-scale industrial production of microbes requires growing them in what type of vessel?
questions.explanation: Industrial-scale production requires growing microbes in very large vessels called fermentors, which allow controlled large-volume cultivation.

questions.question: Which fungus is used for the commercial production of citric acid?
questions.explanation: Aspergillus niger is a fungus used industrially to produce citric acid. Other microbes produce different organic acids: Acetobacter aceti produces acetic acid, Clostridium butylicum produces butyric acid, and Lactobacillus produces lactic acid.

questions.question: Which bacterium produces acetic acid commercially?
questions.explanation: Acetobacter aceti is the bacterium responsible for the commercial production of acetic acid. It belongs to the group of microbes used for industrial production of organic acids.

questions.question: Clostridium butylicum is used for the commercial production of which acid?
questions.explanation: Clostridium butylicum is a bacterium used for the industrial production of butyric acid. Each microbe has a specific metabolic pathway that leads to a characteristic organic acid product.

questions.question: Which yeast is used for the commercial production of ethanol?
questions.explanation: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's or brewer's yeast) is used commercially to produce ethanol through fermentation. It is the same yeast used in bread-making and beverage fermentation.

questions.question: What is the role of lipases in detergent formulations?
questions.explanation: Lipases are enzymes produced by microbes and are added to detergent formulations because they efficiently break down fats and oils, thereby removing oily stains from laundry. This is one of the key industrial applications of microbially produced enzymes.

questions.question: Why are commercially bottled fruit juices clearer than home-made ones?
options: They are boiled at high temperature
They are clarified using pectinases and proteases
questions.explanation: Commercially bottled juices are treated with enzymes pectinases and proteases, which break down pectin and protein particles that cause cloudiness. This enzymatic clarification makes them visually clearer than freshly prepared home juices.

questions.question: Streptokinase produced by Streptococcus is used as a 'clot buster'. What does it do?
questions.explanation: Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and further modified by genetic engineering, is used therapeutically to dissolve blood clots in the vessels of patients who have suffered myocardial infarction (heart attack).

questions.question: Which fungus produces Cyclosporin A, an immunosuppressive agent used in organ transplants?
questions.explanation: Cyclosporin A is a bioactive molecule produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum. It is used as an immunosuppressive drug to prevent rejection of transplanted organs by suppressing the patient's immune response.

questions.question: Statins produced by Monascus purpureus are used for which medical purpose?
questions.explanation: Statins from the yeast Monascus purpureus are commercially used as blood-cholesterol-lowering agents. They work by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of cholesterol in the body.

questions.question: How do statins lower blood cholesterol levels in the body?
options: By competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis
questions.explanation: Statins act as competitive inhibitors of the enzyme that catalyses the biosynthesis of cholesterol. By blocking this enzyme, statins reduce cholesterol production in the body, making them effective agents against hypercholesterolaemia.

questions.question: What is sewage primarily composed of?
options: Municipal waste water containing human excreta and organic matter
questions.explanation: Sewage is municipal waste water, which contains large quantities of organic matter and microbes, a significant portion of which is human excreta. Many of the microbes present in sewage are pathogenic and pose serious health risks.

questions.question: Why cannot untreated sewage be directly discharged into rivers and streams?
options: It contains organic matter, pathogens and pollutants that harm water bodies
Rivers cannot hold that volume of water
questions.explanation: Untreated sewage is rich in organic matter and pathogenic microbes. Discharging it directly into natural water bodies would pollute water, harm aquatic ecosystems, reduce oxygen levels, and spread water-borne diseases.

questions.question: What is the full form of STP in the context of waste water management?
questions.explanation: STP stands for Sewage Treatment Plant. These are facilities specifically designed to treat municipal waste water using physical, biological, and chemical methods before it is discharged into natural water bodies.

questions.question: Which type of microbes are responsible for treating sewage in sewage treatment plants?
options: Heterotrophic microbes naturally present in sewage
questions.explanation: Sewage treatment relies on heterotrophic microbes that are naturally present in the sewage itself. These organisms break down the organic matter in the waste water through their metabolic activities.

questions.question: What does BOD stand for, and what does a high BOD indicate?
options: Biochemical Oxygen Demand; high organic pollution
Biological Oxidation Degree; low organic matter
questions.explanation: BOD stands for Biochemical Oxygen Demand. It measures the oxygen required to oxidise organic matter in water by bacteria. A high BOD value indicates a high amount of organic matter, meaning the water is more polluted.

questions.question: Which magnification was used to view rod-shaped bacteria as shown in Figure 8.1(a)?
questions.explanation: Figure 8.1(a) shows rod-shaped bacteria magnified at 1500X.

questions.question: At what magnification was the rod-shaped bacterium showing flagella observed in Figure 8.1(c)?
questions.explanation: Figure 8.1(c) shows a rod-shaped bacterium with flagella magnified at 50,000X.

questions.question: Which virus shown in Figure 8.2 causes respiratory infections?

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of sewage treatment plants (STPs)?
options: To make sewage less polluting before disposal
questions.explanation: Sewage treatment plants treat municipal waste water to reduce its polluting potential before it is released into natural water bodies.

questions.question: Which type of microbes are used in the biological treatment of sewage?
questions.explanation: Heterotrophic microbes naturally present in the sewage are responsible for carrying out the biological treatment of waste water.

questions.question: In primary sewage treatment, floating debris is removed by which process?
questions.explanation: During primary treatment, floating debris is removed first by sequential filtration before grit is removed by sedimentation.

questions.question: What is primary sludge in sewage treatment?
options: All solids that settle during primary treatment
questions.explanation: All solids that settle during primary treatment form the primary sludge, while the remaining liquid is called the effluent.

questions.question: What happens in the aeration tanks during secondary sewage treatment?
options: Effluent is agitated and air is pumped in to promote aerobic microbial growth
Chemicals are added to neutralise acids
Water is distilled to remove impurities
questions.explanation: In aeration tanks, the primary effluent is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped in, promoting vigorous growth of useful aerobic microbes into flocs.

questions.question: What does BOD stand for in sewage treatment?
questions.explanation: BOD stands for Biochemical Oxygen Demand, which refers to the amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria.

questions.question: A higher BOD value of waste water indicates:
questions.explanation: The greater the BOD of waste water, the more is its polluting potential, because higher BOD means more organic matter is present which consumes more oxygen.

questions.question: What are 'flocs' in the context of secondary sewage treatment?
options: Masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures
Solid particles removed during primary treatment
questions.explanation: Flocs are masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments that form mesh-like structures; they grow vigorously in aeration tanks and consume organic matter in the effluent.

questions.question: What is activated sludge in sewage treatment?
options: Sediment formed when bacterial flocs settle in the settling tank
questions.explanation: After BOD is significantly reduced, the effluent passes to a settling tank where bacterial flocs sediment; this sediment is called activated sludge.

questions.question: Why is a small part of activated sludge pumped back into the aeration tank?
options: To increase the BOD of the effluent
To serve as inoculum for further biological treatment
questions.explanation: A small part of activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to serve as the inoculum, seeding it with the active microbial community needed for treatment.

questions.question: Where is the remaining major part of activated sludge sent after settling?
questions.explanation: The remaining major part of activated sludge is pumped into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters where anaerobic bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge.

questions.question: Which gases are produced during anaerobic digestion of sludge?
options: Methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: During anaerobic digestion in sludge digesters, bacteria produce a mixture of gases including methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide, collectively called biogas.

questions.question: What is the BOD test a measure of, indirectly?
options: Amount of dissolved salts in water
Amount of organic matter present in the water
questions.explanation: The BOD test measures the rate of uptake of oxygen by micro-organisms in a water sample; indirectly, BOD is a measure of the organic matter present in the water.

questions.question: Where is the effluent from secondary sewage treatment generally released?
options: Back into the primary settling tank
Into natural water bodies like rivers and streams
questions.explanation: After secondary treatment, the treated effluent is generally released into natural water bodies like rivers and streams, as its polluting potential is significantly reduced.

questions.question: For how long has microbial treatment of sewage been practiced worldwide?
questions.explanation: Microbial treatment of sewage has been practiced for more than a century now, in almost all parts of the world, and no man-made technology has been able to rival it.

questions.question: According to the biological farming approach, why is the eradication of pests considered undesirable?
options: Because pests help in pollination of crops
Because beneficial predatory and parasitic insects depend on them as food or hosts
Because pests contribute to soil fertility
questions.explanation: The organic farmer holds the view that the eradication of pests is undesirable because without them, the beneficial predatory and parasitic insects which depend upon them as food or hosts would not be able to survive.

questions.question: Which insects are mentioned as useful to get rid of aphids and mosquitoes respectively?
questions.explanation: The Ladybird beetle with red and black markings and Dragonflies are useful to get rid of aphids and mosquitoes respectively.

questions.question: What is Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) used to control?
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis is a microbial biocontrol agent introduced to control butterfly caterpillars. The toxin released in the gut of larvae kills them while leaving other insects unharmed.

questions.question: In what form are Bacillus thuringiensis spores commercially available?
questions.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis spores are available in sachets as dried spores which are mixed with water and sprayed onto vulnerable plants.

questions.question: How does Bacillus thuringiensis kill the caterpillar larvae?
options: By physically blocking their breathing pores
By releasing a toxin in the gut of the larvae
By causing starvation through leaf destruction
By producing antibiotics that poison the larvae
questions.explanation: In the gut of the larvae, the toxin is released and the larvae get killed. The bacterial disease will kill the caterpillars but leave other insects unharmed.

questions.question: What modern technique has been used to introduce Bt toxin genes into plants?
questions.explanation: Because of the development of methods of genetic engineering, scientists have introduced B.thuringiensis toxin genes into plants making them resistant to insect pests.

questions.question: Which crop is mentioned as an example of Bt toxin gene introduction?
questions.explanation: Bt-cotton is one such example of plants with introduced B.thuringiensis toxin genes, which is being cultivated in some states of our country.

questions.question: Which fungus is being developed as a biological control agent for plant diseases?
questions.explanation: Trichoderma is a biological control being developed for use in the treatment of plant disease. Trichoderma species are free-living fungi common in root ecosystems.

questions.question: Where are Trichoderma species commonly found?
questions.explanation: Trichoderma species are free-living fungi that are very common in the root ecosystems and are effective biocontrol agents of several plant diseases.

questions.question: What type of organisms are baculoviruses?
options: Pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods
questions.explanation: Baculoviruses are pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods. The majority used as biological control agents are in the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus.

questions.question: Which genus of baculoviruses is primarily used as biological control agents?
questions.explanation: The majority of baculoviruses used as biological control agents are in the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of using baculoviruses as biocontrol agents?
options: They have no negative impacts on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects
They are cheaper than chemical pesticides
They can be stored for unlimited time
questions.explanation: Baculoviruses have been shown to have no negative impacts on plants, mammals, birds, fish or even on non-target insects, making them excellent for species-specific insecticidal applications.

questions.question: When is the use of baculoviruses especially desirable?
options: When beneficial insects are being conserved in an IPM programme or in ecologically sensitive areas
questions.explanation: Baculoviruses are especially desirable when beneficial insects are being conserved to aid in an overall integrated pest management programme, or when an ecologically sensitive area is being treated.

questions.question: What does IPM stand for in the context of biological control?
questions.explanation: IPM stands for Integrated Pest Management programme, where beneficial insects are conserved and baculoviruses are used as part of the overall pest control strategy.

questions.question: What is a major environmental concern mentioned at the beginning of the section on biofertilisers?
questions.explanation: With our present day lifestyles, environmental pollution is a major cause of concern, and the use of chemical fertilisers has contributed significantly to this pollution.

questions.question: What has contributed significantly to environmental pollution according to the text?
questions.explanation: The use of chemical fertilisers to meet the ever-increasing demand of agricultural produce has contributed significantly to environmental pollution.
